points: The Massacre of the Acqui Division is also known as the Cephalonia massacre.
German soldiers committed a war crime against prisoners of war from Italy's 33rd Infantry Division, the Acqui Division.
The massacre took place on the Greek island of Cephalonia.
The massacre took place in September 1943, during the Second World War.
The massacre followed the Armistice of Cassibile between Italy and the Allies.
In 1943 the Italian government decided to negotiate a surrender to the Allies.
In response to Italy's move toward surrender, the German Army tried to disarm Italian forces under Operation Achse.
The Acqui Division began resisting the Germans on Cephalonia on 13 September.
The last Italian resistance surrendered on 22 September after running out of ammunition.
The article gives 1,315 as the number of Italians killed in the battle.
The article's main tally puts the number of Italians executed by 26 September at 5,155, or roughly 5,000.
About 3,000 more Italians drowned when ships carrying survivors to concentration camps were sunk.
The Cephalonia massacre was one of the largest massacres of prisoners of war in the Second World War.
The article compares Cephalonia in scale to the Katyn massacre, which the Soviet Union carried out.
The Cephalonia massacre was one of several atrocities committed by the German 1st Mountain Division, also called the 1. Gebirgs-Division.
Greece fell in April and May 1941.
After Greece fell, it was divided into occupation zones.
Italy received most of mainland Greece and most of its islands as an occupation zone.
The Acqui Division had served as the Italian garrison on Cephalonia since May 1943.
The Acqui garrison consisted of 11,500 soldiers and 525 officers.
The Acqui garrison included the 17th and 317th Infantry Regiments.
The Acqui garrison included the 33rd Artillery Regiment.
The Acqui garrison included the 27th Blackshirt Legion, with the XIX Blackshirt Battalion and support units.
The Acqui Division's 18th Regiment was detached for garrison duty on Corfu.
The Acqui Division had naval coastal batteries.
The Acqui Division had torpedo boats.
The Acqui Division had two aircraft.
General Antonio Gandin took command of the Acqui Division on 18 June 1943.
Gandin was 52 years old.
Gandin was a veteran of the Russian Front.
Gandin had earned the German Iron Cross on the Russian Front.
Allied successes helped prompt Germany to reinforce its forces throughout the Balkans.
Germany also reinforced the Balkans because it thought Italy might reach an agreement with the Allies.
Lieutenant Colonel Johannes Barge arrived on Cephalonia on 5–6 July with 2,000 men from the 966th Fortress Grenadier Regiment.
Barge's force included Fortress Battalions 810 and 909.
Barge's force brought a battery of self-propelled guns.
Barge's force brought nine tanks.
After the armistice, Gandin faced a choice between surrendering to the Germans and resisting them.
German forces had prepared for the Italian armistice and had already begun disarming Italian garrisons elsewhere.
Gandin initially asked his superiors for instructions.
Gandin initially opened negotiations with Barge.
The Italian armistice was made public on 8 September 1943.
General Carlo Vecchiarelli commanded the 170,000-strong Italian occupation army in Greece.
Vecchiarelli sent Gandin orders by telegram on 8 September.
Vecchiarelli's orders largely copied General Ambrosio's headquarters directive, known as promemoria 2.
Vecchiarelli ordered the Italians not to attack unless the Germans attacked them first.
Ambrosio told the Italians not to join forces with Greek partisans.
Ambrosio told the Italians not to join forces even with the Allies if they arrived on Cephalonia.
General Pietro Badoglio's directive called for responding decisively to threats from any side.
Vecchiarelli's order implied that the Italians should defend themselves against a German attack but did not say so explicitly.
At 22:30 on 8 September, Ambrosio directly ordered Gandin to send most of his naval and merchant vessels to Brindisi immediately.
The order to send the vessels to Brindisi was required by the armistice terms.
By sending the vessels away, Gandin lost a possible means of escape.
After Mussolini's overthrow, Badoglio agreed to place the Italian and German armies under German command.
Badoglio agreed to the united command to appease the Germans.
The command arrangement technically left Vecchiarelli and Gandin under German command even after Italy's armistice with the Allies.
The Germans saw the command arrangement as a justification for treating Italians who disobeyed them as mutineers or francs-tireurs.
The article says that the laws of war at the time treated francs-tireurs as unlawful combatants who could be executed on capture.
Barge met Gandin at 9:00 on 9 September.
At the meeting, Barge misled Gandin by claiming that he had received no orders from German command.
Barge and Gandin liked each other.
Gandin was pro-German.
Gandin liked Goethe.
Ambrosio assigned Gandin to the Acqui Division to get him out of Italy because he feared Gandin might side with Germany against the plot to depose Mussolini.
Barge and Gandin ended their 9 September meeting on good terms.
Barge and Gandin agreed to wait for orders.
Barge and Gandin agreed that the situation should be resolved peacefully.
On 11 September, the Italian High Command explicitly told Gandin to regard German troops as hostile.
On 11 September, the Italian High Command ordered Gandin to resist German attempts at disarmament with weapons.
On 11 September, Barge gave Gandin an ultimatum with three choices.
One option in Barge's ultimatum was to continue fighting on Germany's side.
One option in Barge's ultimatum was to fight against the Germans.
One option in Barge's ultimatum was to hand over weapons peacefully.
Gandin discussed the ultimatum with his senior officers and the Acqui Division's seven chaplains.
All of Gandin's senior officers and six chaplains advised him to comply with the German demands.
One chaplain advised immediate surrender.
Gandin believed that joining the Germans would violate the Italian king's orders as relayed by Badoglio.
Gandin was reluctant to fight the Germans because they had previously fought alongside the Italians.
Gandin believed that handing over the weapons would violate the spirit of the armistice.
Gandin continued negotiating with Barge despite the Italian High Command's orders to resist disarmament.
Gandin agreed to withdraw his troops from Mount Kardakata, a strategically important position on Cephalonia.
In exchange for the withdrawal, the Germans promised not to bring reinforcements from the Greek mainland.
On 12 September, Gandin told Barge that he was prepared to surrender the Acqui Division's weapons.
Barge reported Gandin's willingness to hand over the weapons to his superiors in the XXII Mountain Corps.
Gandin's junior officers pressured him not to make a deal with the Germans and threatened mutiny.
The detached Acqui regiment on Corfu was not under Gandin's command.
Around midnight on 12–13 September, the detached regiment on Corfu radioed Gandin to say it had rejected an agreement with the Germans.
Gandin received reports he considered credible that surrendered Italian soldiers were being deported rather than sent home.
On 13 September, a five-ship German convoy approached Argostoli, the island's capital.
Italian artillery officers ordered the remaining batteries to fire on the convoy on their own initiative.
The Italian fire sank two German landing craft.
The attack on the convoy killed five Germans.
On the night of 13 September, Gandin polled his troops on choices broadly based on Barge's ultimatum.
The poll offered the troops the option of joining the Germans.
The poll described surrender as a way for the troops to be sent home.
The poll offered the troops the option of resisting the Germans.
A large majority of the Italian troops favored resistance.
The exact size of the majority for resistance is unknown.
Following the poll, Gandin backed out of the agreement to hand over the division's weapons on 14 September.
Gandin was willing to hand over only the division's heavy artillery.
Gandin told the Germans to leave Cephalonia.
Gandin demanded a German reply by 9:00 on 15 September.
When negotiations stalled, the Germans prepared to resolve the crisis by force.
A German ultimatum to the Italians expired at 14:00 on 15 September.
On the morning of 15 September, the Luftwaffe began bombing Italian positions with Stuka dive-bombers.
The Italians initially had the advantage on the ground.
The Italians took about 400 Germans prisoner.
German reinforcements called Battle Group Hirschfeld landed on Cephalonia on 17 September.
Major Harald von Hirschfeld commanded the reinforcement group.
Battle Group Hirschfeld included the III./98 and 54th Mountain Battalions of the 1st Mountain Division.
Battle Group Hirschfeld included the I./724 Battalion of the 104th Jäger Division.
The article describes the German 1st Mountain Division as an elite unit.
The 98th Gebirgsjäger Regiment had been involved in atrocities against civilians in Epirus in the months before the Acqui massacre.
Around the time the reinforcements landed, the Germans dropped leaflets urging the Italians to surrender.
The German leaflets claimed that the Italian leaders had betrayed their troops.
The German leaflets promised the Italians a way home if they laid down their arms.
Gandin repeatedly asked the Italian Ministry of War in Brindisi for help but received no reply.
Gandin sent a Red Cross emissary to seek help from the Ministry of War.
The emissary's mission broke down off the coast of Apulia.
The mission reached the Italian High Command in Brindisi three days later, too late to help.
Three hundred aircraft loyal to Badoglio were based at Lecce in southern Italy.
The aircraft at Lecce were within range of Cephalonia and ready to intervene.
The Allies prevented the aircraft from intervening because they feared the aircraft might defect to the Germans.
The Allies ordered two Italian torpedo boats already headed for Cephalonia to return to port because they feared those boats might also defect.
Local residents helped the Italian troops.
Small detachments of the Greek ELAS partisan organization helped the Italian troops fight.
The Germans had complete air superiority during the battle.
Experienced German troops had an advantage over the Italian conscripts of the Acqui Division.
The Italian withdrawal from Mount Kardakata gave the Germans another strategic advantage.
After several days of fighting, the last Italians surrendered at 11:00 on 22 September on Gandin's orders.
German sources put German battle losses at 300.
German sources put Italian battle losses at 1,200.
Fifteen Greek partisans were killed fighting alongside the Acqui Division.
The article dates the start of the massacre to 21 September, before the last Italian resistance surrendered.
The article says the massacre lasted one week.
Hitler had issued an order allowing the summary execution of Italian officers who resisted, on grounds of treason.
On 18 September, the German High Command ordered that no prisoners be taken on Cephalonia.
The German High Command justified its no-prisoners order by accusing the Italians on Cephalonia of treachery.
German mountain troops began executing Italian prisoners in groups of four to ten.
In the first phase, German soldiers machine-gunned surrendering Italians where they stood.
A group of Bavarian soldiers objected to the killings.
The Bavarian soldiers who objected were themselves threatened with summary execution.
The Germans marched remaining Italian prisoners to the San Teodoro town hall.
The prisoners taken to the town hall were executed by eight-member detachments.
Gandin and 137 senior officers were summarily court-martialed on 24 September.
Gandin and the 137 senior officers were executed.
The bodies of Gandin and the executed senior officers were discarded at sea.
General Luigi Gherzi was the division's infantry commander.
Gherzi was executed immediately after his capture on 22 September, while fighting was still underway.
Romualdo Formato was one of the Acqui Division's seven chaplains and one of the few survivors of the massacre.
Formato wrote that Italian officers cried during the massacre.
Formato wrote that Italian officers prayed during the massacre.
Formato wrote that Italian officers sang during the massacre.
Formato recalled many officers calling out the names of their mothers, wives, and children.
Formato recalled three officers embracing and saying that they had been comrades in life and would go to paradise together in death.
Formato recalled other officers digging through the grass as if looking for a way to escape.
Formato recalled Germans calling out an offer of medical help to wounded Italians.
According to Formato, about 20 wounded men crawled forward in response and were killed by machine-gun fire.
Officers entrusted their belongings to Formato for delivery to their families in Italy.
The Germans confiscated the belongings entrusted to Formato.
Formato could no longer account for the exact number of officers killed.
While officer executions were continuing, a German officer spared Italians who could prove they came from South Tyrol.
Hitler had annexed South Tyrol as a German province after 8 September.
Formato appealed to the German officer to save the remaining Italian officers.
The German officer said he would consult his commanding officer about Formato's appeal.
The German officer returned after about half an hour and told Formato that the executions of officers would stop.
Thirty-seven Italian officers survived, counting Formato.
After the reprieve, the Germans congratulated the remaining Italians.
The Germans offered the remaining Italians cigarettes.
The reprieve did not end the danger to the remaining Italians.
After the reprieve, the Germans forced 20 Italian sailors to load the dead officers' bodies onto rafts and take them out to sea.
The Germans blew up the rafts with the Italian sailors still aboard.
Alfred Richter was an Austrian participant in the massacre who later gave an account of it.
Richter recalled an Italian soldier who had sung arias for Germans in local taverns.
According to Richter, that soldier was forced to sing while his comrades were executed.
The singing soldier's fate is unknown.
Richter said he and his regimental comrades felt a delirium of omnipotence during the massacre.
Most of the soldiers in Richter's German regiment were Austrians.
Richter said the Italians were killed after surrendering to soldiers of the 98th Regiment.
Richter said the bodies were thrown into heaps.
Richter said the men whose bodies were heaped up had all been shot in the head.
Soldiers of the 98th Regiment took boots from the corpses for their own use.
Richter recalled groups of Italians being taken to quarries and walled gardens near Frangata and executed by machine-gun fire.
The killings near Frangata lasted for two hours.
The shooting and the victims' screams could be heard inside homes in Frangata.
Some victims' bodies were burned on large wooden pyres.
The burning bodies produced a strong smell across the island.
Some bodies were taken aboard ships for burial at sea.
Survivor Amos Pampaloni said some Italians were executed in Argostoli harbor on 23 September 1943 in full view of the Greek population.
Pampaloni said the bodies of those executed in the harbor were left where they fell.
Pampaloni said the smell of decomposing bodies in smaller streets was so strong that he could not stay long enough to take a photograph.
Some bodies were thrown into the sea with rocks tied to them.
The Germans refused to allow Acqui soldiers to bury their dead.
A chaplain searching for bodies found bones scattered across the island.
Local residents and ELAS helped the few soldiers who escaped the killings.
A taxi driver took one badly wounded survivor to the home of a Cephalonian woman.
That wounded soldier survived the war and went on to live at Lake Como.
The ships carrying Italian prisoners to concentration camps were the Sinfra, Mario Roselli, and Ardena.
The article attributes the sinking of the prison transports to Allied air raids and sea mines in the Adriatic.
Hitler instructed local German commanders to omit safety precautions when transporting prisoners, regardless of losses.
The article attributes the transport deaths in part to that German policy.
The article also links similar transport losses among Italian garrisons in the Dodecanese to that German policy.
A book review in Corriere della Sera reported alternative estimates of between 1,650 and 3,800 Italians massacred on Cephalonia.
Similar killings of surrendered Italian troops took place on a smaller scale elsewhere.
The Italian garrison on Corfu consisted of 8,000 troops from parts of three divisions.
German forces landed on Corfu on 24 September.
The German landing on Corfu was codenamed Operation Treason.
The Italian garrison on Corfu capitulated by 25 September.
All 280 Italian officers on Corfu were executed in the two days following the surrender.
General Lanz ordered the executions on Corfu in accordance with Hitler's directives.
The bodies of the Corfu officers were loaded aboard a ship and disposed of at sea.
After the Battle of Kos, between 96 and 103 Italian officers were shot along with their commander.
By October 1943, Mussolini had been freed and had established a new Fascist republic in northern Italy.
In October 1943 the Germans gave the remaining Italian prisoners a choice between fighting for Germany, doing forced labor on Cephalonia, and going to concentration camps in Germany.
Most of the remaining Italian prisoners chose forced labor on Cephalonia.
A chaplain's account of the events reached Benito Mussolini in January 1944 after Aurelio Garobbio informed him of the massacre.
Garobbio was a Swiss Fascist from the Italian-speaking canton of Ticino.
Mussolini was angry that the Germans had carried out the massacre.
Mussolini regarded the Acqui officers as traitors more than he did their soldiers.
Garobbio complained to Mussolini that the Germans had shown no mercy.
In response to Garobbio, Mussolini praised the Italians for defending themselves and sinking German landing craft.
Hirschfeld was never tried for his role in the massacre because he did not survive the war.
Hirschfeld became the Wehrmacht's youngest general officer in December 1944.
Hirschfeld was killed in 1945 while fighting at the Dukla Pass in Poland.
General Hubert Lanz was Hirschfeld's superior commander.
Lanz was the only person sentenced for the Cephalonia massacre.
Lanz received a 12-year prison sentence in the Southeast Case of the Nuremberg Trials.
Lanz was also sentenced for his troops' involvement in other atrocities in Greece.
The other atrocities covered by Lanz's sentence included the massacre at Kommeno on 16 August 1943.
Lanz was released from prison in 1951.
Lanz died in 1982.
Barge was not on Cephalonia while the massacre was taking place.
Barge was later awarded the Knight's Cross of the Iron Cross.
